ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Gauging in Salt Lake City, UT
ut.description: UT inspection in Salt Lake City, UT: thickness surveys on refinery piping, vessels and tanks plus shear wave weld examination. Send your scope for a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Salt Lake City, Utah
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Salt Lake City refineries, plants, fabrication shops and rail yards for ultrasonic thickness surveys on piping and vessels and for shear wave examination of welds. The work follows a written procedure approved by an ASNT Level III, and the report names the code used for acceptance. Send the components and the governing code through this UT inspection quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Salt Lake City

The northern Salt Lake Valley is one of the few refining centers in the Rocky Mountain region. The U.S. Energy Information Administration counts five refineries in the Salt Lake City area with a combined crude capacity of roughly 206,000 barrels per calendar day, close to a third of the regional total, and much of the crude arrives by pipeline from Utah, Colorado, Wyoming and Canada. Inside those plants, ultrasonic testing answers a simple question over and over: how much wall is left?

Typical Salt Lake City scopes include:

  • Overhead and reflux piping on crude and vacuum units, where wall loss concentrates at elbows, tees and injection points.
  • Exchanger shells, heater inlet piping, drums and desalter vessels that carry a recorded thickness history.
  • Aboveground storage tank shell courses and nozzle necks on crude and product tanks.
  • Steam, condensate and boiler feedwater lines at refineries, hospitals, universities and district heating plants.
  • Structural members, crane runway girders and process equipment in the copper mining, smelting and refining operations on the west side of the valley.
  • Groove welds in pressure piping, pipe racks and fabricated vessels built by shops along the Wasatch Front.

Thickness surveys: how corrosion is actually tracked

A thickness survey is only useful when the same spots are read the same way each time. In a Salt Lake City refinery the owner's inspection group usually marks condition monitoring locations on a piping isometric or a vessel sketch, and our technician returns to those marks. Corroded or pitted surfaces call for a dual-element probe, because a single-element probe can lose the back wall on a rough surface. The instrument is calibrated on a step block of the same material, and the technician watches the A-scan so a doubled echo or a lamination is recognized rather than recorded as a false reading.

Hot lines need a high-temperature probe and couplant rated for the surface, plus a temperature correction to the velocity. The method is described in ASTM E797 and in ASME Section V Article 23 (SE-797); our plain-language walk-through is in ultrasonic thickness measurement requirements. Where the line has insulation, the owner cuts inspection windows or removes sections so the probe touches bare metal.

What a Salt Lake City thickness record shows for each location
FieldWhy it matters
Location ID and grid positionLets the next survey repeat the exact point
Nominal and minimum required wallFrames the reading against the design
Measured wall and surface temperatureShows the corrosion trend and the correction applied
Calibration block and instrumentTies the number to a checked setup

Shear wave examination of welds in Salt Lake City

Weld examination uses an angle-beam probe, commonly 45, 60 or 70 degrees, that sends shear waves through the weld volume. The technician builds a reference level or distance-amplitude curve from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, scans the weld from both sides where access allows, and evaluates reflectors against the acceptance table in the governing code. Lack of fusion, cracks and slag show up as reflectors with a position, length and amplitude that can be plotted.

The procedure traces to ASME Section V Article 4, and the acceptance rules come from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping, AWS D1.1 Clause 8 for structural groove welds, or AWS D1.5 where the owner is a highway agency and the weld is on a steel bridge. Where an owner wants ultrasonic examination in place of radiography, the swap is written into the specification before work starts; see our national ultrasonic testing service for scope detail.

What UT finds and what it misses

Ultrasound is strong on planar flaws and wall loss and weaker in a few situations that matter in this valley. Coarse-grained castings and austenitic stainless welds scatter the beam and make reflectors hard to separate from noise. Rough scale, flaking paint and pitting change coupling and can hide a real reading. Reflectors lying nearly parallel to the beam may go unseen, and sizing a crack by amplitude alone is an estimate rather than a measurement.

The near-surface region is another blind spot: a dead zone under the probe face means thin sections and surface-breaking flaws may need a second method. In those cases the right answer is often magnetic particle or liquid penetrant testing alongside UT, and the report states exactly what was and was not covered.

Codes, regulators and the Utah boiler regime

Most Salt Lake City refining work is governed by owner programs built on API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for tanks. Under those codes the owner's authorized inspector holds responsibility for the inspection; Atlantis performs the ultrasonic work and hands over thickness and flaw data. OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), expects mechanical integrity inspections to follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and PHMSA rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 apply to transmission pipelines.

Utah also regulates boilers and pressure vessels at the state level. The Utah Labor Commission's Boiler, Elevator and Coal Mine Safety Division administers rule R616-2, issues a Certificate of Inspection and Permit to Operate for compliant equipment, and sets intervals by vessel type; for example, the rule lists 48 months for most other pressure vessels under the Division's jurisdiction. Insurance company deputy inspectors and owner-user inspection programs also operate under that framework. Our UT data feeds whoever signs the inspection record.

Preparing the component for ultrasonic examination

Good readings start with a clean surface. For thickness work the probe needs bare metal or a thin, well-bonded coating that the procedure has been checked against; loose scale, rust jackets and blistered paint should be wire-brushed or ground smooth at each location. For weld scans the technician needs a flat strip beside the weld wide enough for the probe to travel, usually measured in multiples of the metal thickness, and the weld cap may need to be dressed if its profile prevents coupling.

Before a survey, send the owner's isometrics, vessel drawings, previous thickness data and any known damage mechanisms such as sour water, naphthenic acid or chloride cracking. That history tells the technician where to put extra readings, which matters in a refinery where a handful of locations drive the remaining-life calculation. Scaffolding, lighting and a safe place to set the instrument down belong in the plan as well.

Who performs the work and how they are qualified

Technicians are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, which is an employer-based system. A Level II sets up and calibrates the instrument, performs the examination and interprets the result. An ASNT Level III approves the ultrasonic procedure and reviews reports; the Level III on the company's practice is founder Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

If you run your own program, a procedure or written practice review is a separate service: see written practice development and outsourced Level III consulting.

What the UT report contains

A usable ultrasonic report lets someone who was not on the job repeat it. Ours lists:

  • Component or weld identification, drawing or isometric reference and the code governing acceptance.
  • Procedure number and revision, probe type, frequency, angle and couplant.
  • Instrument, calibration block, calibration checks and surface temperature.
  • Technician name and qualification level, with the reviewing Level III.
  • For welds, each reflector with location, length, amplitude and an accept or reject call; for thickness work, the grid or location table with readings and remaining wall.
  • Any area not examined and the reason, such as access, insulation or surface condition.

Planning a UT job in Salt Lake City

The city sits near 4,200 feet and swings from freezing winter nights to hot, dry summer afternoons. Cold changes couplant behavior and instrument battery life, so low-temperature couplant and warm equipment storage are part of a winter plan. In summer, steel in direct sun can run hot enough to need high-temperature probes. Refinery turnaround windows in spring and fall fill up quickly, so share dates early.

Atlantis keeps no office in Salt Lake City. Technicians travel to your site from outside the area, so allow for site badging, safety orientation, confined space entry permits and scaffold or rope access arranged by the owner. Tell us the line size, insulation, surface temperature and the code up front, and the quote will reflect the actual job rather than a generic day.

A sample UT scope for a Salt Lake City refinery

A typical request: an overhead line on a distillation unit has a history of thinning at the elbows, and the owner wants thickness readings on a grid at each elbow and the straight runs between them ahead of a spring turnaround. The scope names line sizes, insulation type, expected surface temperature, the previous readings, and the minimum required wall. Our technician records readings on the marked locations, flags any below the limit, and delivers a table the owner's inspector can use for a corrosion rate and remaining life calculation.

Ultrasonic, magnetic particle or penetrant testing in Salt Lake City

Choose ultrasonic testing when the question is wall thickness or something inside the weld. Choose magnetic particle inspection for surface cracks on carbon steel welds and structural details, and liquid penetrant testing for stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals. Many Salt Lake City scopes combine two: a UT thickness survey plus MT on the welds that were repaired. For a plain-language overview, see the ultrasonic testing guide.

Training your own UT technicians

If your plant wants its own ultrasonic technicians, Atlantis trains to the SNT-TC-1A recommendations. Start with UT Level 1 training or UT Level 2 training, practice on the UT practical simulator, and see NDT training for Salt Lake City for how delivery works. Your employer certifies under its own written practice.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic testing cost to schedule in Salt Lake City?
faq.a: Each job is quoted from its scope: number of locations, line sizes, insulation, access, applicable code and travel to your site. Atlantis publishes no standard rates because a thickness survey on twenty locations and a weld examination on a vessel are different jobs. Send the details through the quote form and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on welds in Salt Lake City?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 contain ultrasonic provisions, and Section VIII allows it under specific conditions. The substitution has to be agreed with the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector before work begins.

faq.q: How do you take thickness readings on hot piping?
faq.a: We use high-temperature probes and couplant rated for the surface, calibrate on a step block, apply a temperature correction and record the surface temperature next to each reading, so later surveys can be compared fairly.

faq.q: Do you have an office in Salt Lake City?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized from outside the city to your refinery, plant or yard for the agreed scope. Plan for badging, orientation and permits on your side, and tell us the schedule when you request the quote.

faq.q: Which codes does the UT report reference?
faq.a: The report cites the examination procedure, usually based on ASME Section V Articles 4, 5 or 23, and the acceptance code that governs the item: ASME VIII, B31.3, API 510, 570 or 653, AWS D1.1 or D1.5.

faq.q: Who is responsible for the inspection under API 510, 570 and 653?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and reports thickness and flaw data that the inspector uses for the record and the remaining life decisions.

faq.q: What stops ultrasonic testing from working on a component?
faq.a: Heavy scale, rough or coated surfaces without access to bare metal, coarse-grained castings and austenitic welds, very thin walls, and flaws oriented along the beam. The report records anything that could not be examined.

faq.q: Does Utah require inspection of pressure vessels?
faq.a: Yes. The Utah Labor Commission's Boiler, Elevator and Coal Mine Safety Division administers rule R616-2 and issues a Certificate of Inspection and Permit to Operate for compliant boilers and pressure vessels within its jurisdiction.

faq.q: Can my team learn ultrasonic testing instead of buying the service?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and Level 2 training aligned to SNT-TC-1A and a browser-based practical simulator, so people can rehearse calibration and flaw evaluation before touching real equipment. Your employer then certifies technicians under its own written practice.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Salt Lake City, UT
mt.description: Mag particle testing in Salt Lake City, UT: weld, crane, vessel and structural steel MT with yoke or wet fluorescent methods. Send your scope for a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Salt Lake City, Utah
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Salt Lake City sites for magnetic particle inspection of carbon and low-alloy steel: pressure vessel and piping welds, crane and hoist components, mining and smelter structural steel, and rail and fabrication work. Examinations follow a procedure written to ASME Section V Article 7 or the owner's code, and every indication is located, sized and called accept or reject. Use this MT inspection quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Salt Lake City

Magnetic particle inspection earns its place wherever steel is stressed, welded or repaired, and the Salt Lake Valley has plenty of all three. The refineries on the north side of the valley run carbon steel vessels, piping and tanks that need surface crack checks after weld repair or alteration. The copper mining and smelting operations on the valley's west side lean on heavy lifting and haulage equipment, where fatigue cracks start at welded brackets and pin bosses. Rail yards along the Union Pacific corridor, fabrication shops, and steel framing for the city's construction boom round out the demand.

Frequent MT targets here include:

  • Weld seams, nozzle attachments and repair areas on carbon steel pressure vessels and process piping.
  • Shell-to-bottom and nozzle welds on aboveground storage tanks after repair.
  • Crane hooks, shackles, lifting lugs and runway beam welds where a fatigue crack is a safety event.
  • Structural connections and weld toes on pipe racks, equipment frames and platforms.
  • Fabricated assemblies awaiting final acceptance in shops along the Wasatch Front.

What MT finds and what it cannot

MT works by magnetizing the part and applying fine ferromagnetic particles that gather where a discontinuity leaks magnetic flux. It is strong on surface-breaking cracks and on flaws just under the surface, such as lack of sidewall fusion at a weld toe. It works on ferromagnetic material only: carbon steel and most low-alloy steel yes, austenitic stainless, aluminum and copper alloys no. Because copper and stainless are common at smelters and process plants in this area, we confirm the base metal before committing to the method.

Orientation matters. A crack is found best when the field crosses it at close to a right angle, so the code calls for two examinations with the field in roughly perpendicular directions. Heavy paint, scale or weld spatter reduce sensitivity, and deep subsurface flaws are out of reach. When the answer needs to be about the inside of the weld, UT is the better tool; ultrasonic testing in Salt Lake City covers that.

Techniques used on Salt Lake City jobs

For most field work the technician uses an electromagnetic yoke with articulated legs, which magnetizes without burning the surface and can be walked along a weld. ASME Section V Article 7 requires an AC yoke to lift at least 10 pounds (4.5 kg) at the maximum pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds (18 kg); the technician checks this with a test weight before the job. Prods can drive a stronger field through a thick section, but they risk arc burns on finished surfaces, so many owners restrict or forbid them.

Particles come as dry powder for rough, hot or outdoor work, or as a wet suspension for higher sensitivity. Fluorescent wet particles are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, which in daylight means a shroud or tent; visible wet particles on a thin white contrast coating are the practical choice on many outdoor tanks and vessels. After examination, parts that will be welded, machined or placed in service next to sensitive equipment are demagnetized and checked for residual field.

Codes and acceptance criteria that apply in Salt Lake City

The method comes from ASME Section V Article 7, supported by ASTM E1444 and the guide in ASTM E709. Acceptance comes from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 for structural steel. For API 510, 570 and 653 repairs and alterations, the owner's authorized inspector decides acceptance of the repair; our report gives that inspector the indication data.

Utah's Labor Commission, through its Boiler, Elevator and Coal Mine Safety Division, oversees boilers and pressure vessels under rule R616-2, so weld repairs on regulated equipment normally follow the National Board Inspection Code. OSHA process safety management also expects mechanical integrity work to follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice. For a plain-language reading of the method standard, see Article 7 requirements explained.

Surface preparation and contrast

Magnetic particles collect only where they can move, so a weld that is wet with oil, caked with scale or covered in spatter will not give a reliable indication. The usual preparation is a wire brush or light grinding of the weld and about an inch of adjacent base metal, followed by a solvent wipe so the carrier or powder can reach the surface. For visible wet work the technician applies a thin white contrast coating first, which turns a dark particle line into something a reviewer can photograph and evaluate.

Roughness is a trade-off. A very rough surface traps particles and creates false indications, while a polished one can make dry powder skid. The procedure states the acceptable surface condition, and the technician records when a location was examined as found rather than cleaned.

Typical findings and how they are handled

Most MT indications on Salt Lake City jobs fall into a few families: crack-like lines at weld toes, linear indications from lack of fusion at the sidewall, laps and seams in rolled shapes, arc strikes and grinding marks. Not every line is a defect. Under the acceptance table in the construction code, rounded indications below a stated size are allowed while any linear crack-like indication is rejected, and relevant indications are measured so the owner can see how close each one is to the limit.

When a crack is found, the usual path is to grind it out under the owner's repair procedure, then re-examine the ground area with MT to confirm the crack is gone before welding. If grinding removes more than the allowed wall, a thickness check by ultrasonic testing follows. Each step is documented so the repair record reads as a continuous story rather than a pile of separate reports.

A sample MT scope for a Salt Lake City refinery repair

A typical request reads like this: a carbon steel vessel nozzle was replaced during a spring shutdown, and the owner wants magnetic particle examination of the new nozzle-to-shell weld, the repair pad welds and the adjacent lifting lugs. The scope names the procedure, the acceptance code, the surface temperature expected, and how scaffolding will be provided. Our technician examines the welds in two perpendicular directions with a calibrated yoke, records indications, and hands the owner's inspector a report ready for the repair package.

Mining and heavy equipment around Salt Lake City

The copper operations on the west side of the valley and the construction industry along the Wasatch Front use some of the heaviest equipment in the state. Haul truck frames, shovel components, crusher structures, rail loading equipment and tower cranes all carry welded steel under repeated load. Cracks in those parts usually start at welded brackets, pin bosses and sharp transitions, and magnetic particle inspection is the routine way to check them during maintenance windows.

Because the parts are large and the work is often outdoors, the technician combines a yoke for the welds with dry powder for rough or hot surfaces, and records the position of every indication on a sketch. Owners use the results to decide whether a crack can be ground out in the field or whether the component needs a shop repair.

Who does the work

MT is performed by technicians qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, in which the employer certifies its personnel. A Level II sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications; an ASNT Level III approves the written procedure and reviews reports. If your own program needs a procedure written or a practice reviewed, we offer written practice development and Level III consulting.

What the MT report contains

  • Component or weld ID, drawing reference, material and governing code.
  • Procedure number and revision, technique (yoke, prods or coil), current type and particle type.
  • Yoke lifting check, light readings for fluorescent work, and equipment identification.
  • Technician name and level, with the Level III who reviewed the report.
  • Each indication with location, length and orientation, sketched or photographed, and the accept or reject decision against the named criteria.
  • Demagnetization result where it was required.

Planning an MT job in Salt Lake City

Salt Lake City is dry and high, which helps contrast but brings its own issues. Winter nights drop well below freezing, and cold steel changes how wet carriers flow and how long a contrast coating takes to dry, so the procedure has to cover the actual surface temperature. In summer, steel in direct sun can get hot enough to evaporate a wet carrier before the indication forms, which pushes the work toward dry powder or early-morning starts. Dust from dry weather and windblown grit also affects surface cleanliness.

Atlantis keeps no office in Salt Lake City, so technicians travel to your site with their own yokes, lights and test blocks. Plan for refinery badging, hot-work and confined-space permits, access scaffolding and a place to set up shade or a darkening tent. Spring and fall turnaround seasons fill quickly, so give us the dates when you request the quote.

MT, PT or UT for your Salt Lake City job

Pick magnetic particle testing for surface cracks on carbon steel welds, lifting gear and fatigue-critical details. Pick liquid penetrant testing in Salt Lake City for stainless steel, aluminum or any non-magnetic part, and ultrasonic inspection for wall thickness or internal weld flaws. If you are unsure, the MT versus PT comparison explains how to choose, and our national MT service page lists the standard scope.

Training your own MT technicians

A plant that wants to run its own crack checks can start with MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and see NDT training for Salt Lake City for delivery options. Practice questions are available in the NDT practice tests library. Certification stays with the employer under its written practice.

faq.q: What materials can magnetic particle inspection be used on?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic materials: carbon steel and most low-alloy steels. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and titanium cannot be magnetized, so liquid penetrant testing is used on those materials instead. The technician confirms the base metal with a magnet or the material records before any examination starts.

faq.q: Is yoke magnetization enough for pressure vessel welds in Salt Lake City?
faq.a: Often yes. A yoke that meets the lifting power check in ASME Section V Article 7 works for most welds. Thick sections, large castings or special geometry may call for prods or coil techniques written into the procedure.

faq.q: Can MT be done on painted steel?
faq.a: Thin, well-bonded coatings may be acceptable if the procedure has been demonstrated through them, but heavy or flaking paint reduces sensitivity. The usual practice is to strip the coating at the weld and adjacent base metal before examination.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a crew in Salt Lake City?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized from outside the city to your refinery, plant, yard or shop for the agreed scope, so travel, badging and permits are part of the plan and the quote.

faq.q: How is a fluorescent MT examination done outdoors?
faq.a: The area is shaded or enclosed so ambient white light stays low enough for the procedure, UV-A intensity is measured at the surface, and the technician allows time for eye adaptation before evaluating indications. Fluorescent work in open daylight without shade is not acceptable under the usual procedure.

faq.q: When is demagnetization needed?
faq.a: When residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining, instrument operation or cleanliness of moving parts. The technician checks the part with a field indicator or gauss meter and records the residual field in the report, along with any additional treatment that was needed to bring it below the limit.

faq.q: Which codes apply to MT on piping and vessels?
faq.a: The method is ASME Section V Article 7. Acceptance usually comes from ASME B31.3 for process piping, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for pressure vessels, or AWS D1.1 for structural steel.

faq.q: Does Utah require inspection of repairs on pressure vessels?
faq.a: Utah's Labor Commission administers boiler and pressure vessel rules under R616-2, and repairs on regulated equipment generally follow the National Board Inspection Code. Your authorized inspector or the state inspector decides what a repair requires.

faq.q: How do I get MT technicians trained for my own plant?
faq.a: Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and Level 2 training aligned to SNT-TC-1A, with practice tests. Your employer then certifies trained people under its own written practice and checks their qualification records.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Salt Lake City, UT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Salt Lake City, UT: stainless, aluminum and nickel welds, tubesheets and castings, visible or fluorescent dye. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Salt Lake City, Utah
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Salt Lake City plants and shops for liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, on stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and other non-magnetic metals where magnetic particle testing cannot be used. Penetrant also works on carbon steel when a surface-breaking crack must be confirmed. Procedures are written to ASME Section V Article 6, or to whichever code the owner names. Describe the parts and the code in this PT inspection quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Salt Lake City

Penetrant testing fits the mix of industries around the Salt Lake Valley. Refineries and chemical plants use stainless and alloy steel in heat exchangers, heater tubes and corrosion-resistant piping, and penetrant is the standard check for weld toes and tubesheet welds on those materials. Food, dairy and beverage plants rely on stainless sanitary piping. Copper and metals processing equipment uses nickel and stainless alloys. Fabrication shops along the Wasatch Front weld aluminum frames, trailers and process skids, and penetrant is the final surface check before they ship.

Typical Salt Lake City PT work includes:

  • Austenitic stainless piping welds and vessel nozzle welds in process and utility service.
  • Exchanger tubesheet and shell welds, and repair areas after retubing.
  • Aluminum and nickel alloy fabrications built by shops in the valley.
  • Castings, forgings and machined parts checked for surface cracks before service.
  • Weld repairs on carbon steel when the owner prefers penetrant to magnetic particle for a specific geometry.

What penetrant finds, and what it needs

PT finds only discontinuities that are open to the surface: cracks, laps, porosity breaking the surface, and cold shuts. A low-viscosity liquid is drawn into the opening by capillary action, excess is removed, and a developer pulls the liquid back out so the flaw appears as a visible line or dot. It works on any non-porous material, magnetic or not, which is why stainless steel, aluminum and titanium depend on it.

The limits are just as real. A flaw that is closed by smeared metal from grinding, blasting or machining will not take up penetrant, so the surface may need etching before the test. Porous surfaces bleed and hide indications. Anything sub-surface, however serious, will not appear. If the question is a flaw inside the weld, the right method is ultrasonic testing in Salt Lake City rather than penetrant.

Technique: from cleaning to evaluation

The sequence is the same on every job even if the materials change. The surface is cleaned and dried; penetrant is applied and left to dwell for the time in the procedure; excess penetrant is removed; developer is applied; and the area is examined after the development time. Field work in Salt Lake City most often uses a solvent-removable visible-dye system, where the penetrant is red and the developer is a white spray, because it needs no water, power or darkened space. Fluorescent penetrant, viewed under UV-A light in a dark area, is chosen where higher sensitivity is needed, such as critical stainless welds and aluminum castings.

Dwell and developing times come from the procedure and depend on the material and the expected defect. The technician keeps to these times and does not let developer dry unevenly, because both are common causes of missed or false indications. Residues are removed after the test so they cannot interfere with later welding or with process service.

Temperature, contamination and the Salt Lake City climate

ASME Section V Article 6 sets the standard range for the part and the penetrant materials at 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit (5 to 52 degrees Celsius). A job outside those limits needs a procedure that has been qualified for the temperature actually met on site. That is a daily concern here: winter mornings in the valley sit below the lower limit, and steel that has baked in the summer sun can exceed the upper one. Heating a cold part gently or shading a hot one is often the practical answer, and the temperature is recorded.

Chemistry matters as well. For nickel alloys, austenitic stainless steel and titanium, the penetrant materials are controlled for halogens and sulfur so that residues cannot cause cracking or attack in service. The technician uses lot-certified materials and keeps the batch records with the job file. These controls are part of why penetrant testing is quoted as a procedure, not as a spray can.

Codes and acceptance criteria

Penetrant procedures come from ASME Section V Article 6, supported by ASTM E165 for general industry and the material specifications the owner selects. Acceptance depends on the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 for structural welds. In general, any linear indication that is crack-like is rejected, while rounded indications are measured against a size limit.

Utah regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Labor Commission's Boiler, Elevator and Coal Mine Safety Division under R616-2, and repairs on regulated equipment follow the National Board Inspection Code. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner's authorized inspector accepts the repair; our penetrant report supplies the data. For a plain-language reading of the method, see Article 6 requirements explained.

Surface preparation and when etching is needed

Penetrant can only reveal what it can enter, so cleaning matters more than any other step. Oil, paint, scale and process deposits are removed with solvent and abrasive pads, then the part is left to dry so no cleaner remains inside a crack. Utah's dry air helps here, though dust and windblown grit settle on cleaned steel quickly, so cleaning and application happen in sequence on small areas rather than across a whole structure at once.

Smeared metal is the hidden trouble. Grinding, wire wheels and machining can close a surface crack, and the penetrant then has nowhere to go. When the surface history suggests smearing, the procedure calls for etching or light conditioning, followed by neutralizing and full drying. Stainless steel in food and dairy plants adds sanitation checks, so the owner's quality staff approve any chemical used.

Visible or fluorescent penetrant

Visible dye penetrant shows as red on a white developer and can be read in ordinary light, which suits outdoor refinery work and quick weld checks. Fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light and detects finer cracks, making it the choice for critical stainless welds, aluminum castings and machined components. Because fluorescent work needs a darkened area and a calibrated light, it is more often a shop procedure, although tents and shrouds make field use possible.

The two systems are not interchangeable mid-job. Penetrant, remover and developer must be compatible families, and the procedure names the combination approved for the work.

Typical findings and how they are handled

PT indications on Salt Lake City work include crater cracks at weld ends, toe cracks, surface porosity, laps in forgings, and fine fatigue cracks at machined features. Each relevant indication is measured, and the acceptance table of the governing code decides whether it passes. Doubtful indications are wiped away and retested to see whether they return in the same place, which separates real cracks from surface residue.

Confirmed cracks are removed by grinding under the owner's repair procedure, the area is re-examined, and welding proceeds only once the surface is clean of indications. A final examination after the repair weld closes the record.

A sample PT scope for a Salt Lake City heat exchanger

A typical request: a stainless steel exchanger at a process plant has been retubed during a spring shutdown, and the owner wants penetrant testing of the tube-to-tubesheet welds and the repaired shell weld. The scope gives the procedure, the acceptance code, the material grades and the access plan. Our technician applies penetrant with contamination-controlled materials, evaluates each weld, records every indication, and delivers a report the owner's inspector can attach to the repair package.

Who performs penetrant testing and how it is reviewed

Technicians are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, which leaves certification with the employer. A Level II performs the test and evaluates indications; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. To have a penetrant procedure written for your plant or your written practice reviewed, see written practice development and Level III consulting.

What the PT report contains

  • Component or weld ID, material, drawing reference and governing code.
  • Procedure number and revision, penetrant type and method, developer type and the lot numbers used.
  • Surface temperature, dwell time and development time.
  • Technician name and level, with the reviewing Level III.
  • Each indication with location, size and a photograph or sketch, and an accept or reject decision against the code.
  • Post-cleaning confirmation where service conditions call for it.

Planning a PT job in Salt Lake City

Atlantis keeps no office in Salt Lake City, so technicians travel to your plant, shop or yard with consumables, lights and test blocks. Tell us the material, surface temperature, the area to be examined and whether the work is in a clean-service or food-grade environment, where residue control is stricter. Wind and dust in the valley can contaminate a cleaned surface between steps, which is why large outdoor areas are often broken into sections and worked one at a time.

Turnaround windows in spring and fall are busy, and owners often want penetrant work to follow welding and grinding promptly, so share the schedule early. Badging, safety orientation, confined-space permits and access arrangements are on your side and are part of the plan we agree before the technician travels.

Large exchanger bundles and tall vessels bring access issues of their own: a technician may need a platform, a lift or a manway entry, and each of those carries its own permit. The plan covers who provides lighting, who watches the confined space, and where used penetrant materials go, since waste handling follows the plant's rules.

PT, MT or UT for your Salt Lake City job

Use penetrant for stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and any non-magnetic surface, and for confirming a crack on carbon steel. Use magnetic particle inspection for carbon steel welds where speed and sensitivity at the toe matter, and ultrasonic testing for thickness or internal flaws. The MT versus PT comparison helps decide, and the national penetrant testing service page lists standard scope.

Training your own PT technicians

Teams that want their own penetrant capability can begin with PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, rehearse the steps on the penetrant testing simulator, and see NDT training for Salt Lake City for delivery options. The employer certifies technicians under its written practice.

faq.q: What is the difference between liquid penetrant and dye penetrant testing?
faq.a: They are the same method. Dye penetrant refers to the visible red dye system, while fluorescent penetrant is viewed under UV-A light. Both detect only flaws open to the surface and follow the same cleaning, dwell, removal and developing steps.

faq.q: Which metals need penetrant instead of magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys, nickel alloys and titanium cannot be magnetized, so liquid penetrant testing is the usual surface method for them. It also works on carbon steel when preferred.

faq.q: Can PT be done in a Salt Lake City winter?
faq.a: Yes, if the part and materials are within the procedure temperature range, normally 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit under ASME Section V Article 6. Cold parts are warmed gently, or a procedure qualified at the lower temperature is used.

faq.q: Does Atlantis keep staff stationed in Salt Lake City for penetrant work?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized from outside the city to your plant, shop or yard, so travel, access and schedule are agreed when you request the quote.

faq.q: What surface preparation does penetrant testing need?
faq.a: The surface must be clean, dry and free of oil, scale, paint and weld spatter. Grinding, blasting or machining that smears metal over cracks may require etching before the test so flaws are open to the surface.

faq.q: Why are penetrant materials controlled for halogens and sulfur?
faq.a: On nickel alloys, austenitic stainless steel and titanium, residues from penetrant materials can cause cracking or corrosion. Lot-certified materials with low halogen and sulfur content are used and recorded in the job file.

faq.q: Which codes cover penetrant testing of welds?
faq.a: The method is ASME Section V Article 6, with acceptance from ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 or AWS D1.1, depending on the work. ASTM E165 supports general industry use.

faq.q: Who accepts a weld repair on a pressure vessel in Utah?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector or the state inspector, depending on the equipment. Utah's Labor Commission administers boiler and pressure vessel rules under R616-2, and the National Board Inspection Code governs repairs.

faq.q: Can my staff learn penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 and Level 2 training aligned to SNT-TC-1A and a penetrant testing simulator, and your employer certifies people under its own written practice.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in Salt Lake City, UT: What We Offer
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States. Salt Lake City, UT buyers can get UT as a volumetric alternative and Level III radiograph review.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Support in Salt Lake City, Utah
rt.html:
Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, in Salt Lake City or anywhere else. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity: the Nuclear Regulatory Commission sets the rules in 10 CFR Part 34, and Utah, as an Agreement State, administers its own radiation control rules for the same work. We do not hold a source license and we do not offer to shoot film or images here. If you searched for RT in Salt Lake City, this page explains what Atlantis can do for you instead.

Why Atlantis does not offer radiography in Salt Lake City

Radiography uses sealed gamma sources or X-ray tubes, and the people who operate them must be licensed, trained as radiographers, and covered by a radiation safety program. Exclusion zones, source security and records are all regulated. A company that does not hold that license cannot lawfully offer the service, so Atlantis does not. If your specification requires radiography on a weld or casting, you will need a licensed radiography contractor, and the owner or the engineer should choose one against the contract requirements.

Ultrasonic testing as a volumetric alternative in Salt Lake City

Where the construction code and the owner allow it, ultrasonic examination can replace radiography for the volumetric check of a weld. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 gives ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII permits ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only under specific conditions. None of these substitutions is automatic. The owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector agree before the job that ultrasonic examination is acceptable for the specific weld.

When that agreement exists, our Level II technicians travel to your site and perform shear wave examination to a procedure approved by an ASNT Level III. See ultrasonic testing in Salt Lake City for what the examination covers, and our national UT service for scope. Surface checks at the same weld are available as magnetic particle inspection and liquid penetrant testing.

Level III review of radiographs and RT procedures

Review work does not need a radiation license because no source is used. Our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and Atlantis can support Salt Lake City owners with:

  • Independent review of radiographs, in film or image form, and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code.
  • A second read on disputed or borderline indications before a weld is cut out.
  • Review of a radiography contractor's procedure and written practice before they begin work.

Send the images and the code through this radiograph review request and we reply within one business day. For program-level help, see Level III consulting and written practice development.

Radiography theory training

If your team wants to understand radiography, we teach the theory behind it, including image quality, exposure principles and interpretation, in RT Level 2 training. Theory instruction is not a substitute for a radiographer license or for employer-based certification, which remains with the employer under its written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A.

Planning with Atlantis in Salt Lake City

Atlantis keeps no office in Salt Lake City. Technicians are mobilized from outside the city to your refinery, plant or shop for the agreed scope, and Level III review is done remotely from the images you send. Tell us the material, thickness, code and what the radiography contract requires, and we will say plainly which part we can help with.

faq.q: Why does Atlantis not perform radiographic testing in Salt Lake City?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States because it is a licensed activity under NRC rules in 10 CFR Part 34 or the equivalent Agreement State rules, and we do not offer it.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my weld?
faq.a: Only when the construction code permits it and the owner accepts it. Get the engineer and authorized inspector to sign off on ultrasonic examination for that specific weld before the job, and have the procedure cite the governing code.

faq.q: Can Atlantis review radiographs from another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review radiographs and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, and give a second read on disputed indications. No radiation license is needed for review work.

faq.q: Does Atlantis teach radiography?
faq.a: Atlantis teaches radiographic testing theory in its RT Level 2 course. The course does not license anyone to operate sources, and employer certification remains under the employer's written practice.

faq.q: How do I request a Level III radiograph review?
faq.a: Use the review request link on this page and attach images or describe the code and weld. We reply within one business day and say whether the review fits our scope.
